topic: DP-3T: The Privacy-First Secret Whisper for Contact Tracing
target_audience: University students (Computer Science, Data Privacy, or Public Health Tech)

sections.title: The Privacy Dilemma: The Health vs. Privacy Trade-off
sections.content: Introduce the challenge of tracking a virus without creating a 'Big Brother' surveillance state. Define the goal: How can Bob know he was exposed to Alice without a central server knowing where Alice and Bob were or who they are?
sections.example: Visual: Two characters, Alice and Bob, walking in a park. A central 'Eye' (Server) tries to watch them, but DP-3T puts a fog between the Eye and the citizens.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Cryptographic Hashes & BLE
sections.content: Briefly explain two building blocks: 1. One-way Hash Functions (transforming data into a unique string that can't be reversed). 2. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) 'Beacons' (short-range digital handshakes).
sections.example: Visual: A 'Meat Grinder' icon representing the Hash function. Input 'Secret' -> Output 'f3a2...'. Show a smartphone emitting a small blue ripple to represent a BLE beacon.

sections.title: Step 1: Local Key Generation (The Secret Seed)
sections.content: Explain the hierarchy of keys generated locally on the phone. Every day, a phone generates a Temporary Exposure Key (TEK). From this, it derives Rolling Proximity Identifiers (RPIs) that change every 15 minutes to prevent tracking.
sections.example: Graphic: A 'Tree' diagram. Root = Secret Key (SK). Branch = Daily Key (TEK). Leaves = RPI_1, RPI_2... RPI_n (changing like a digital camouflage).

sections.title: Step 2: The Digital Handshake (Whispering in the Crowd)
sections.content: When Alice and Bob are near each other, their phones exchange RPIs via Bluetooth. They store these 'random-looking' numbers locally on their own devices. No location data or names are exchanged.
sections.example: Visual: Alice's phone sends 'ID_Alpha' to Bob. Bob's phone sends 'ID_Beta' to Alice. Both phones save these IDs in a local 'Digital Diary' that stays on the phone.

sections.title: Step 3: Notification & Decentralized Matching
sections.content: If Alice tests positive, she voluntarily uploads her Daily Keys (TEKs) to a public server. Bob’s phone periodically downloads these keys. Bob’s phone then locally recalculates the possible RPIs from those keys and checks if they match any IDs in his 'Digital Diary'.
sections.example: Animation: Alice uploads a 'Key' to a cloud. Bob's phone downloads it and runs a 'Match' process. If a match is found, Bob sees a 'Risk of Exposure' alert, but the server never knows Bob was the one who matched it.

sections.title: Summary: Why it Works
sections.content: Recap the decentralized nature: The server only acts as a 'bulletin board' for keys. The actual 'matching' happens on the user's device, ensuring the government never knows who met whom.
sections.example: Conclusion Image: A shield protecting a group of people. The text overlay: 'Decentralized = Privacy by Design'.
